newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus parliament, president on collision course.
newsitem.headline: Belarus parliament, president on collision course.

text.p: The Belarus parliament, setting itself on a collision course with President Alexander Lukashenko, voted on Friday to go ahead with a referendum on November 24 that could abolish the post of president altogether.
Deputies voted by 88 to 84 in favour of conducting the poll shortly after Lukashenko stormed out of the chamber vowing to hold a separate referendum designed to extend his mandate.

The 41-year-old Lukashenko, who has been accused by critics of taking an increasingly authoritarian line since coming to power two years ago, told parliament he had withdrawn proposals intended to appease deputies opposed to his referendum.

He reaffirmed his resolve to go ahead with the plebiscite on November 7 -- anniversary of the 1917 Bolshevik revolution. It will seek approval for a new constitution which would give him a new five-year tenure into the next century.
"I will go directly to the people and I will withdraw my initiative, and the people will be our judge," he said.
"I do not see any opportunity to find a compromise in this parliament," Lukashenko said.
Lukashenko had held out an olive branch on Thursday by offering deputies wider powers if they shelved plans for their referendum on a separate constitution.
But his offer drew little support and the head of the constitutional court said Lukashenko's referendum could lead to the establishment of a dictatorship.
"Tomorrow we will have a totalitarian regime in the centre of Europe, with the castration of our parliament and the constitutional court," said Valery Tikhinya.
"We, the Constitutional Court, do not have the right to stay silent in this extreme situation," Tikhinya said.
He added that Lukashenko's constitutional project had divided the former Soviet republic of 10 million into groups for and against his constitution.

Lukashenko, who has suspended trade unions, closed newspapers and effectively halted market reforms since being elected first post-Soviet president in 1994, said he was withdrawing his offer of compromise to his opponents.
Lukashenko, who frequently addresses Belarus's people at length on state television, said he would go ahead with an "All-Belarus Meeting" on October 19 to seek backing for his plebiscite.
Opposition members said the meeting will be attended only by functionaries loyal to Lukashenko.
Lukashenko has said that Russian President Boris Yeltsin had expressed support for his planned referendum. The two leaders are due to meet next Wednesday in Moscow.
